title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: AGE TAKES AVOIR: elle a trente ans, not elle est trente. L1-M9 already shipped an and ans, so only the verb choice is new — and it is the single most reliable English error in French. Features take avoir too: il a les cheveux bruns, elle a les yeux verts.

A POSSESSIVE AGREES WITH THE THING POSSESSED, not with the owner. sa voiture is his car AND her car; son frère is her brother AND his. English marks the owner and French marks the noun, so a learner hunting for a masculine word to mean "his" gets it exactly backwards — the gender in the sentence belongs to what is owned.

Before a vowel the FEMININE possessive borrows the masculine shape: mon amie, ton école, son adresse. It is not a gender change — amie is still feminine — it is that French will not put ma in front of a vowel. The sound decides the spelling, which is the same instinct behind bel and vieil in the next module.

The article goes where English wants a possessive: il a les cheveux bruns, never ses cheveux, in this frame. Whose hair it is was never in doubt, so French does not say it — the same habit Italian and Spanish both have.

Two words carry two jobs each and no second row can take them back. femme is "woman" and "wife"; fille is "girl" and "daughter". Only the sentence around them says which, and both notes are written true of both readings.

words.note: The third-person cell of avoir, beside L1-M5's ai and avez. One letter, and the à with an accent is a different word entirely.
The final e is silent but it is what stops the t before it from disappearing too — trente ends in a t sound and vingt does not.

sentences.trap: elle est trente is what an English speaker says and it means nothing. In French you HAVE your years, and the noun ans can never be dropped.
sentences.sound: el a TRAHNT ahn. The an of ans is nasal, and the s is silent.

mistake.why: Age is had: Elle a trente ans.

sentences.usage: Saying how old someone is, which comes up early in every conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: You have your years, you do not be them.

words.note: PLURAL in French — the hairs — so its adjective is plural too. The singular cheveu is one single hair.
For hair and eyes. marron is the everyday brown for objects and does not agree at all, being a noun — a chestnut.

sentences.trap: There is an article where English has a possessive. il a LES cheveux is what is said, and ses cheveux in this frame would sound as though somebody else's hair were also in question.
sentences.sound: eel a lay shuh-VUH BRUHN. The eux is a rounded vowel with no consonant after it.

variations.changed: a woman — and the adjective follows the hair, not her

mistake.why: The article does the work: Il a les cheveux bruns.

sentences.usage: Describing someone so they can be found in a crowd.
sentences.mnemonic: French has THE hair, not YOUR hair.

words.note: Its singular is œil, which shares no letters with it at all. That is the most irregular plural in the language and it simply has to be learnt.
Four cells. The t is silent in the masculine and sounded in the feminine — verte — which is how most French adjectives work.
Its masculine plural is also gris, because it already ends in s. Adjectives ending in s or x never take another one.

sentences.trap: œil and yeux are the same word and look nothing alike. The ligature œ is one letter and must be written — writing oeil would make it a different word to the index.
sentences.sound: el a lay-ZYUH VER. The s of les links onto the y and is heard as a z.

variations.changed: a colour that does not add an s

mistake.why: The adjective follows yeux: Elle a les yeux verts.

sentences.usage: The other half of a description, after the hair.
sentences.mnemonic: œil and yeux — one word, two shapes, no overlap.

words.note: It agrees with what is owned. mon frère whoever is speaking — the owner's own gender never enters it.
ma sœur, ma voiture. Before a vowel it becomes mon — mon amie — because French will not say ma before a vowel.
One form for both genders in the plural: mes frères, mes sœurs. The plural is always the easy cell in this system.
The è takes a grave accent, which is a letter and not decoration — frere would be a different key entirely.
The third-person plural of être, and Ce sont is what introduces more than one person — C'est goes singular, Ce sont goes plural, and English uses "this is" for both.

sentences.trap: The possessive is chosen by frère and by nothing else. A woman saying this still says mon frère, because the word agrees with the brother.
sentences.sound: say mon FREHR. The on of mon is nasal, and the è is an open e.

variations.changed: plural, and the verb moves too

mistake.why: frère is masculine: C'est mon frère.

sentences.usage: Introducing family, or handing round a photograph.
sentences.mnemonic: The possessive agrees with what is owned.

words.note: One word for both, because it agrees with the thing. son frère is her brother AND his, and nothing in the sentence says which.
sa voiture is his car and her car alike. English marks the owner here and French refuses to.
The plural, and still silent about the owner. ses enfants is his children or hers.
One word for a boy or a girl, and its article does the gender work: un enfant, une enfant. It never changes shape for sex.

sentences.trap: This is the module's real delta and it is worth saying twice: sa voiture does not mean "her car". It means the car of somebody, and the a is there because voiture is feminine.
sentences.sound: say sa vwa-TÜR. The ur ends in the rounded ü, not the oo of English.

variations.changed: a masculine thing — and still silent about the owner

mistake.why: voiture is feminine: C'est sa voiture.

sentences.usage: Talking about a third person's things or family.
sentences.mnemonic: The gender in the sentence is the thing's, not the owner's.

words.note: Mon ami can mean a boyfriend as well as a friend, and the context decides. Un ami is the safer way to say the second thing.
Feminine, and it still takes MON — mon amie — because it starts with a vowel. The word has not changed gender; the sound has forced the spelling.

sentences.trap: mon amie is feminine. That is the whole point of the rule, and a learner who reads mon as a gender signal will get this wrong every time it appears.
sentences.sound: say mon-na-MEE. The n of mon links onto the vowel and is fully sounded, which is the clue that a vowel follows.

variations.changed: a male friend — spelled one letter shorter, said the same
the tu possessive, borrowing the same shape
plural, where the rule does not apply at all

mistake.why: A vowel takes mon: C'est mon amie.

sentences.usage: Introducing someone, and the shape that trips every learner once.
sentences.mnemonic: The sound decides, not the gender.

words.note: The tu possessive, and it follows mon's rules exactly — including borrowing its shape before a vowel, as in ton amie.
ta sœur, and tes for the plural. The whole set mirrors mon, ma, mes with a t.
The neutral word. papa is what a child says and what an adult says warmly, exactly as in English.
The l is silent in the masculine and the feminine gentille ends in a soft y sound. Same word, two quite different endings.
Short for sympathique and invariable in speech — il est sympa, elle est sympa. It is the everyday compliment, where gentil is about kindness specifically.
Plural by default. It also means "relatives" in older and formal use, which is where the English word came from.

sentences.trap: Character goes to être, and only age and features go to avoir. Il est gentil but il a trente ans — and the split is by what is being said, not by the person.
sentences.sound: ton PEHR eh treh zhon-TEE. The final l of gentil is not sounded.

mistake.why: Character takes être: Ton père est très gentil.

sentences.usage: Talking about someone's family to them.
sentences.mnemonic: être for what you are, avoir for years and features.

words.note: The œ is ONE letter and must be written as one — soeur would be a different key. The vowel is rounded and open, close to the eu of cheveux.
The masculine ends in a nasal vowel with no t sounded; the feminine intelligente sounds the t. That is the ordinary French pattern.
père's pair, with the same grave accent. maman stands beside it as papa stands beside père.

sentences.trap: The ligature is not a typographic flourish. sœur and soeur are two different surfaces to the index, and only one of them has a row behind it.
sentences.sound: ma SUHR eh treh zan-tay-lee-ZHONT. The feminine ending is where the t finally gets said.

mistake.why: The adjective agrees: Ma sœur est très intelligente.

sentences.usage: Describing family, which is what these words are mostly for.
sentences.mnemonic: Write the ligature. It is one letter.

words.note: One word for both, and only the sentence says which. Its spelling lies about the sound: it is said FAM, with an a.
Only "husband" — the word for a man is homme. So the pair femme/mari is not symmetrical, which is worth noticing.
grand's opposite, and one of the few adjectives that goes BEFORE its noun: une petite maison. M3 gives the list.

sentences.trap: femme is said FAM and not FEM. It is the one word in the course where an e is pronounced as an a, and no rule covers it.
sentences.sound: ma FAM eh puh-TEET. The feminine petite sounds its t; the masculine petit does not.

variations.changed: the adjective in front of the noun

mistake.why: The adjective agrees: Ma femme est petite.

sentences.mnemonic: femme is said with an a.

words.note: Two jobs on one word, like femme. The ll is a soft y — FEE-yuh — and the word for a son is fils, said FEESS with the l silent.
The l is silent and the s IS sounded, which is backwards from every other French word. Its plural is also fils.
It ends in e already, so the feminine adds nothing. Adjectives like this have only two written forms.
Its feminine is vieille, which shares almost nothing with it. M3 adds the third shape, vieil, for the vowel case.

sentences.trap: fils and fille look like a pair and sound nothing alike: FEESS and FEE-yuh. The l is silent in one and a y in the other, which is as unhelpful as French spelling gets.
sentences.sound: sa FEE-yuh eh ZHUHN. The ille is the soft y, and jeune ends in the rounded vowel.

mistake.why: fille is feminine: Sa fille est jeune.

sentences.mnemonic: fils sounds its s; fille sounds a y.
